item.title: How often should a transformer be maintained and what should be checked first?
item.description:
Routine inspection frequency depends on environment and load severity, but most projects use monthly visual checks, quarterly operational checks, and annual comprehensive maintenance.

For oil-immersed units, priority items include oil level, oil quality, leakage points, winding temperature, and abnormal noise. For dry-type units, focus on ventilation channels, dust buildup, terminal tightness, and hotspot alarms.

Any sudden temperature rise, unusual vibration, or repeated protection trips should trigger immediate diagnostics rather than waiting for the next scheduled maintenance cycle.

item.title: How do I choose the right transformer capacity for my project?
item.description:
Start from measured or estimated load profile instead of summing all nameplate loads directly. Distinguish base load, normal operating load, and short-duration peak load to avoid oversized or undersized selection.

A common engineering approach is to keep a reasonable future margin, often around 15% to 25%, and verify voltage drop and temperature rise under worst-case operating conditions.

If your load includes large motor starts, frequent impact loads, or fast expansion plans, it is better to evaluate with detailed power quality and thermal calculations before finalizing capacity.

item.title: What is the difference between an oil-immersed transformer and a dry-type transformer?
item.description:
Oil-immersed transformers use insulating oil for heat dissipation and insulation, so they usually have stronger overload capability and are often used outdoors, in substations, and in higher-capacity distribution systems.

Dry-type transformers use air and epoxy resin insulation, with no oil leakage risk, making them more suitable for indoor applications such as commercial buildings, hospitals, and data centers where fire safety and cleaner operation are priorities.

In practice, selection should consider installation environment, capacity requirement, fire protection standard, and lifecycle maintenance strategy rather than only initial equipment cost.
